ideas.name: straight-line parallel jaw (Roberts four-bar with parallel guide)
ideas.description: The servo horn drives one rocker of a Roberts straight-line four-bar: two equal 50 mm rockers on mr63 bearings in the gripper body and a triangular printed coupler. The coupler point traces a nearly straight horizontal line across the opening; the deviation can be held under about 2 mm over 20-95 mm of fingertip separation. A second link parallel to one rocker keeps the finger plate vertical, so the face stays parallel at every opening. The whole linkage sits beside and above the moving finger, outboard of the grip gap. Unlike long_slide, no rack or gear sector spans the space over the object. Squeeze is servo torque over an effective lever of about 45-50 mm, roughly 32-36 N at 1.62 N*m. That is comparable to the slide at r=47-50, which already gained gelatin, pudding and tuna.
ideas.test: Model the four-bar as a jaw type: rocker length, coupler geometry and pivot positions in the gripper body. Run the interference check over the full servo range and all wrist rolls (the long_slide sector at r=50 failed this check). Report the fingertip's rise and the face angle across 17-96 mm openings. proposals.edit: jaw -> long_slide (sector_radius_mm=50)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (gelatin, pudding, sugar, mustard, tuna) and the related fixed_jaw_missed / squeezed_down_out. On the stock hinge, by the time the jaw is open wide enough for these objects (0.68-0.83 rad, 69-79 mm) the moving fingertip has risen +11 to +17 mm above the fixed one, and its face is tilted 44-53 deg. On these low objects (tops at +15 to +29 mm from centre) the moving tip comes down on the top edge, pushing 67-86 deg down, and the fixed jaw either barely touches or never reaches the side.
proposals.principle: A finger on a swinging joint rises by about R(1-cos q) and its face turns with q. A finger can only hold a side if its tip reaches below the object's top, and only horizontal, opposed normals hold. A straight slide has no rise and no turn at any opening.
proposals.hypothesis: long_slide at sector_radius_mm=50 gives fingertips up to 103 mm apart, which covers mustard at 96 mm, the widest. Per the brief, at 35, 55 and 85 mm the face stays at 0 deg, the tip at +1 mm and the squeeze at 32 N, against 20 N on the stock jaw. Both tips then go down the sides of the 30-58 mm tall boxes and cans and press horizontally. Friction: sugar weighs 5.0 N, and 2*0.5*32 = 32 N holds it easily. Mustard: 2*0.4*32 = 26 N against 4.2 N. Tuna: 2*0.35*32 = 22 N against 1.7 N. Arm load: 0.41 + 0.15*5.14 = 1.18 N*m, plus about 0.1 for the slide's mass, still under the 1.62 N*m stall. No params move helps, because rise and tilt are fixed by the hinge geometry: System 1 already tried every close target. Prismatic tops out at 68 mm even with 60 teeth, and parallelogram link 90 still rises +33 mm at 85 mm, so neither is enough. Cost $6.40 (4 rods and bushings), 3 days, 216 machine minutes, all within budget.
risks: dice / large_marker (17-19 mm): at 50 mm per rad the close target is coarse, but the squeeze is higher and the faces are parallel, so these should still hold.

Rolling objects (apple, golf_ball, tennis_ball, lemon, plum, strawberry, racquetball, tomato_soup_can): they are held today with tilted faces. With parallel faces and no rise both contacts sit at the equator, which should hold them at least as well, but a sphere is not centred by flat faces, so System 1 must place the grasp at mid-height.
The extra wrist mass is small next to the 0.44 N*m torque margin.
proposals.result: refused before trial: mechanism law (no interference): the wrist and the pinion share material, a region up to 1.6 x 0.2 x 0.5 mm (jaw at -0.17 rad, wrist rolled -2.74..-2.74 rad); parts may share material only at a bearing seat, within 10 mm of the hinge axis

iterations.notes:
I've sent three body changes for the six failing objects. The simulator hasn't tried any of them yet, so which groups they gain is only my prediction.

**Diagnosis.** The gelatin box, pudding box, sugar box, mustard bottle and tuna can all fail the same way: the stock jaw is on a hinge. To open the 69–79 mm these objects need, the jaw turns 0.68–0.83 rad. By then its fingertip has risen 11–17 mm above the fixed one and its face is tilted 44–53 deg. These objects are low (their tops are only 15–29 mm above centre), so the moving fingertip lands on the top edge and pushes down at 67–86 deg instead of gripping the side. No close setting fixes this, because the rise and tilt come from the hinge itself, and System 1 has already searched the close targets.

The potted meat can is a different failure. Both jaws grip only its top 4 mm, on metal with friction 0.35, and it slid out after rising 28 mm.

**1. Swap the jaw for `long_slide`, sector radius 50 mm.** This is the only catalogue part that reaches wide enough without the rise:
- It opens to 103 mm, enough for the 96 mm mustard bottle.
- At every opening the face stays at 0 deg, the fingertip at +1 mm, and the squeeze at 32 N (the stock jaw gives 20 N).
- The heaviest object, the 514 g sugar box, puts about 1.18 N·m on the shoulder, plus about 0.1 for the slide. That is under the 1.62 N·m stall.
- The other options fall short. `prismatic` opens only 68 mm even with 60 teeth. `parallelogram` at 90 mm links still rises 33 mm at an 85 mm opening.
- It costs $6.40 for the rods and bushings, 3 days lead time and 216 machine minutes.
- It should gain the five low, wide objects.

**2. Add `pads` on the current hinge: TPU skin 1.5 mm, reach 5 mm, pad angle 0.** It costs nothing; everything is on hand. The TPU doubles the face friction (0.9 instead of 0.45), and the 5 mm reach lets the fingers grip the can a little lower while adding only about 2 deg of tilt. This targets the potted meat can.

**3. Both together: the long slide plus TPU pads with 10 mm reach.** On a slide, longer pads don't tilt the faces, so they can reach deeper. This one is there in case proposal 2 breaks a held object on the hinge, which would stop the two from ever being tried together.

**Risks to objects that already pass:**
- **Rolling objects** (golf ball, tennis ball, apple, soup can and the others) currently hold with tilted faces. Parallel faces at their middle should hold them at least as well, but flat faces don't centre a ball.
- **Dice and marker** (17–19 mm): the slide closes 50 mm per radian, which makes their close target coarser.
- **Mustard bottle** in proposal 3: the pads take a few mm off the 103 mm maximum opening, which leaves little clearance for the 96 mm bottle.

**Budget:** each proposal that uses the slide spends $6.40 of the $40 left, and proposal 3 needs 232 of the 600 machine minutes.

On the slide, a second problem took over: rack_on_top_face. The rack stands about 33 mm above the fingertip, so it pressed down on the tops of the banana (+20 mm, top at +19), the tomato can (+33, top at +34) and the apple.
proposals.principle: A finger can hold a side only if everything on it stays below the object's top only where it should. The fingertip has to reach below the top, and the rest of the hand has to clear it. Extending the pads downward moves the contact lower relative to the rack.

It lost apple, banana and tomato_soup_can only because the rack hit their tops, and potted_meat_can was lost at the force limit. With reach_mm going from 5 to 30, the pads hang 25 mm further below the rack. For the same contact height the rack then sits at about 58 mm above the fingertip, so it clears the banana (38 tall), and System 1 can grasp the apple and tomato can at the equator with the rack above their 68-72 mm tops. r=49.5 stays under the interference limit: 49.6 passed, 49.9 was refused. No revolute parameter fixes the tip rise, and pad_angle 40 already failed (it lost banana and potted_meat_can). The record never tried changing the slide's pads, which is why this is not a repeat. Cost: $6.40, 3 days, about 216 + 30 machine min.

proposals.edit: pads (pad_angle_deg=40)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face / squeezed_down_out. On the hinged jaw the moving face is far from parallel at wide openings. The brief gives 47 deg at 75 mm, 56 deg at 85 mm and 66 deg at 95 mm, bottom swung out. The trials show the moving pad touching the object's top corner and pushing down at 49-84 deg: gelatin at +12 of +15 mm, 49 deg; pudding at +17 of +19 mm, 84 deg; tuna at +17 of +17 mm, 78 deg. N sin(a) beats friction, so the box is pushed down or the pad rides up onto its top. Squeeze (20 N) and arm torque (0.41 + 0.15*5.14 = 1.18 N*m < 1.62 at 514 g) are not the limit.
proposals.principle: A tilted contact squeezes an object out when tan(a) exceeds friction (cardboard 0.5 means a < ~27 deg; metal 0.35 means a < ~19 deg). A pad tilted back by pad_angle is parallel to the fixed face when the jaw has opened by that angle, so the tilt is moved to where the failing widths are. According to the catalogue rows, pad_angle 45 brings 85 mm from +61 deg / tip +27 mm down to +14 deg / tip +14 mm, and 55 mm from +35 to -8 deg. That is about 1 deg of face and 0.3 mm of tip per degree of pad angle.
proposals.hypothesis: At pad_angle 40, the moving face should sit at about +7 deg at gelatin (73 mm), about +16 deg at tuna (85 mm) and about +21 deg at pudding (90 mm). The fingertip should drop about 12 mm, which puts it below the tops of pudding (+19) and tuna (+17) instead of on them. This is the cheapest rung: a params move with no purchase, only a reprint of the pads (2 g PLA + 1 g TPU, about 18 machine minutes). We already know the long_slide fixes the tilt but loses apple and tomato_soup_can at every reach tried (5 to 30 mm), because the rack hits the tops of tall wide objects, so I am not repeating it. The parallelogram at link 90 would raise the tip to +46 mm at 85 mm, which is worse. Sugar_box (92 mm, about 23 deg) is marginal. Mustard (96 mm) is at the end of the reach and probably not gained.
risks: dice, large_marker, wood_block_cube, flat_screwdriver: at 17-34 mm the moving face goes from +7..+19 deg to about -30..-20 deg (bottom swung in), with the tip about 10 mm lower than the fixed one. That could lift the small object out or touch the table. They are light (5-70 g), and with the TPU skin the fixed face's friction may hold them, but this is the main risk.

mid-width round objects (golf_ball, strawberry, plum, lemon, racquetball, cup, potted_meat_can) go from +25..+35 deg to about -10..-5 deg. That should be neutral to better, but a contact below the equator pushes rollers up.

proposals.edit: pads (groove_mm=0, lip_mm=2, pad_angle_deg=0, pad_tpu_mm=1.5, reach_mm=5, width_mm=12)
proposals.mechanism: squeezed_down_out on gelatin_box. At 0.81-0.87 rad the moving face is about 47 deg off parallel with its bottom swung out. The flat pad face lands on the box's top corner (contact at +12..+13 mm, top at +15), so the contact normal is the tilted face normal, pushing 49-50 deg down. Friction 0.5 cannot hold N sin 49 while the servo keeps closing. The moving tip itself sits below the top (+15 vs the fixed tip), and the fingertips are 74-78 mm apart on a 73 mm box, about 1 mm off the side.
proposals.principle: When a convex edge presses on a flat face, the contact normal is the flat face's normal, not the finger's. A lip at the moving pad's bottom points inward and down along the tilted face normal: 2 mm gives about 1.4 mm horizontally at 47 deg. That reaches the box's vertical side below the top before the tilted face reaches the corner. The contact normal there is horizontal, which makes it antipodal to the fixed jaw's 31 N contact.

idea.name: straight-line parallel jaw (Roberts four-bar with parallel guide)
idea.description: The servo horn drives one rocker of a Roberts straight-line four-bar: two equal 50 mm rockers on mr63 bearings in the gripper body and a triangular printed coupler. The coupler point traces a nearly straight horizontal line across the opening; the deviation can be held under about 2 mm over 20-95 mm of fingertip separation. A second link parallel to one rocker keeps the finger plate vertical, so the face stays parallel at every opening. The whole linkage sits beside and above the moving finger, outboard of the grip gap. Unlike long_slide, no rack or gear sector spans the space over the object. Squeeze is servo torque over an effective lever of about 45-50 mm, roughly 32-36 N at 1.62 N*m. That is comparable to the slide at r=47-50, which already gained gelatin, pudding and tuna.
idea.test: Model the four-bar as a jaw type: rocker length, coupler geometry and pivot positions in the gripper body. Run the interference check over the full servo range and all wrist rolls (the long_slide sector at r=50 failed this check). Report the fingertip's rise and the face angle across 17-96 mm openings. Then run the full 21-object set, checking above all that apple (72 tall), tomato_soup_can (68) and potted_meat_can (84) clear the linkage. Those three were lost on every long_slide body.

iterations.notes:
I'm sending three proposals: two cheap lip settings on the pads, which might fix gelatin_box, and one recorded idea for the four objects the moving fingertip lands on top of.

**What fails.** The moving jaw is hinged, so at the openings these objects need (0.81–1.00 rad) its face tilts 47–56 deg and its tip rises 15–26 mm above the fixed one.
- **gelatin_box** fails differently from the others. Its moving tip is still below the box top, but the flat pad face meets the box's top corner, so it pushes 49–50 deg down and squeezes the box out.
- **pudding_box, sugar_box, tuna_fish_can and mustard_bottle** fail because the moving tip is at or above the top face and presses down on it. No pad setting can make up a 16–26 mm rise.

**Proposals 1 and 2: lip_mm = 2, then lip_mm = 3.** Lip has never been varied; every past pad trial changed only pad_angle. Those three trials gained nothing and each lost potted_meat_can (and banana at 32 and 40 deg), so I am not touching the tilt again. A lip is a small inward hook at the pad's bottom. Its edge should touch the box's vertical side below the top, and an edge pressing on a flat side pushes along the side's normal, which here is horizontal. The two jaws would then push straight against each other. It costs nothing (same 2 g print).
- **Gain predicted:** gelatin_box only.
- **Main risk:** large_marker, a lying 19 mm cylinder, with the 3 mm lip. If the fingertip sits under about 3 mm above the table, the lip could touch the marker below its middle and push it up. That is why lip 2 is the primary proposal.
- **Other held objects:** the round ones are wide enough that a 2–3 mm lip should not touch them. The face angles that hold potted_meat_can and banana are unchanged.

**Proposal 3 (idea, recorded, not tested): a straight-line parallel jaw.** This is a printed four-bar linkage on bearings that moves the moving finger along a nearly straight horizontal line with its face kept vertical.
- **Why the catalogue can't do it:** the long_slide already shows that a jaw which doesn't rise gains gelatin, pudding and tuna. But on every slide body it lost apple, banana and tomato_soup_can because the rack hit their tops. More reach made it worse (it also lost cup, foam_brick, tennis_ball and racquetball), so I am not trying it again. The parallelogram rises even more (+46 mm at 85 mm). The 12 V servos are over budget and don't address this failure.
- **Cost:** 6 × mr63 bearings to buy ($5.40, 3 days). Screws are on hand; about 30 g PLA plus 1 g TPU is about 158 machine minutes.
- **Open questions:** whether it stays straight at the small closed end (dice, marker), whether its squeeze (about 35 N) trips the force limit on potted_meat_can, and whether mustard_bottle (96 mm) is within its travel.

If both lip trials fail, the pads are probably used up as a lever. The top-face objects then need a jaw that doesn't rise and doesn't put anything over the gap, which no catalogue part offers.

iterations.notes:
I've proposed three bodies built on the same move: swap the hinged moving jaw for the long slide and lengthen the pads. None of them has been trialled yet, so the gains below are predictions for the simulator to decide.

**Why the jaw has to change.** On the current hinged jaw the moving fingertip rises as it opens: +16 mm at 75 mm, +24 mm at 85 mm. Its face also tilts 47–56°. That is why gelatin box gets squeezed down and out, and why the jaw lands on the tops of pudding box and tuna can. Five pad-only trials gained nothing. The long slide keeps the face flat (0°, tip +1 mm), and in iteration 6 it gained gelatin box and tuna can, plus pudding box at a radius of 49.2 mm or more.

**Why the slide failed before.** It lost apple, banana and tomato soup can, and potted meat can at radius 49.5. The main cause was the rack pressing down on the object's top. It hit banana at +20 mm with the top at +19, and tomato soup at +33 with the top at +34. So the rack rides only about 33–35 mm above where the pads touch. Potted meat can was also lost to an 18 N side force at radius 49.5, but it held at radius 45.9–47.6.

**The fix.** Longer pads lower the contact point relative to the rack, so the rack clears the tops of these objects. In iteration 3, pads extended 26 mm landed on the tops of cup, foam brick and tennis ball. So I picked 10–17 mm and left room for the loop to fit the pad length and radius:
1. **Radius 47.6, pads 14 mm.** This radius kept potted meat can before. Expected gains: gelatin box, tuna can.
2. **Radius 49.5, pads 17 mm, TPU skin 1.0 mm.** The thinner skin keeps friction at 0.9 and widens the opening slightly for the 90 mm pudding box. Expected gains: gelatin box, tuna can, pudding box.
3. **Radius 48.5, pads 10 mm, 1.5 mm groove.** A cautious hedge; the groove helps keep rolling objects centred on the flat faces. Expected gains: the same three, less surely.

**What it costs.** Each swap needs $6.40 to buy (two bearings and two 150 mm steel rods), 3 days of lead time, and about 216 machine minutes plus about 25 to reprint the pads. That fits within the $40, 7 days and 594 minutes left.

**What none of these fixes.** Sugar box (92 mm) and mustard bottle (96 mm) need an opening wider than about 96 mm with flat faces. The slide reaches about 93 mm at radius 49.5, and radius 50 was refused for colliding with the wrist. Lifting them is not the problem: the arm's torque is enough for both.

proposals.hypothesis: Across the slide trials, reach controls how high the rack sits above the contact. At reach 5 the rack hit banana at +20. At reach 14 banana was kept. At reach 10–17 tomato soup was still hit at +33. At reach 27.8 the rack cleared, and tomato's failure changed to a pad on its top at +29, which also cost cup, foam and tennis. The rack therefore clears tomato and apple somewhere between reach 17 and 27.8. Reach 22 should put the rack about 37–39 mm above the contact, enough to clear apple (36), tomato (34) and banana (19), while leaving the pads 6 mm shorter than the setting that broke cup and foam. Radius 47.6 is the one slide radius that kept potted_meat_can (its squeeze is lower than at 49.5, where the side force hit 18 N), and it opens to about 89 mm. That reaches gelatin (73), tuna (85) and pudding (90, marginal). Sugar (92) and mustard (96) are beyond it. Cheaper moves are exhausted: 5 pad-only trials gained nothing, servos_12v is refused at $68, prismatic tops out at 59 mm, and parallelogram-90 raises the tip 46 mm at 85 mm, worse than the stock jaw. Cost: $6.40, 3 days, about 216 + roughly 60 machine minutes.
risks: potted_meat_can: every slide trial with reach of 10 or more lost it. The failure was a pad pressing on its top rim at about t=0.7 s, or an over-force at t=0.02 s. It is upright and does not roll, so System 1 can grip it high, but this is the most likely loss.
tennis_ball, cup, foam_brick: reach 27.8 lost all three to pads pressing on their tops. Reach 17 lost tennis_ball. Reach 22 sits between those two, so all three are at risk.
apple, tomato_soup_can: this is the bet. If the rack still lands on them at reach 22, this body fails the same way the earlier slide bodies did.

idea.name: outboard-rack long slide (rack and sector behind the moving finger, clear of the jaw gap)
idea.description: This is the long_slide carriage on two 3 x 150 mm rods with an LM3UU bushing per rod. The rack is mounted on the carriage's outboard side, pointing away from the fixed jaw, and the printed sector meshes with it from behind the moving finger. As the jaw closes, the rack retracts outward instead of sliding over the gap. Nothing is then left above the object between the jaws except the rods, which sit above the stock fingertip at full jaw height. The finger still slides straight with its face at 0° and the tip at +1 mm, and squeeze stays at servo torque over sector radius (about 33 N at 48 mm). Short reach-5 pads can be kept, and short pads are what kept cup, foam, tennis and potted meat.
idea.test: The simulator needs a long_slide variant whose rack geometry extends outboard of the carriage, the side away from the fixed jaw, with the sector hub moved behind the moving finger. Then rerun apple, tomato_soup_can, banana and potted_meat_can with reach 5 to confirm the rack no longer lands on their tops, and run gelatin, pudding and tuna to confirm the slide's gains still hold.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face / squeezed_down_out on the low, wide boxes. At 73 to 92 mm the hinged jaw has opened 46 to 60 deg. The moving face sits 47 to 56 deg off parallel with its bottom swung out, and the moving fingertip rides 15 to 26 mm above the fixed one. On gelatin, pudding, sugar and tuna (30 to 45 mm tall) the box's top corner lands on the tilted face, which pushes down at 49 to 84 deg.
proposals.principle: A face that turns with its joint is parallel to the fixed face at only one opening. pad_angle_deg sets that opening. Tilting the moving pad back 45 deg puts the parallel opening at about 0.79 rad, the opening of the failing boxes. Turning the pad also lowers its tip, which works against the R(1-cos q) rise. A tilted contact squeezes the object out only once the tilt is steeper than atan(mu), so a tilt of about 15 deg can be held.
proposals.hypothesis: Brief, pad_angle 45: at 85 mm the face is +14 deg with the tip +14 mm, against +56 deg and +24 mm now. At 55 mm it is -8 deg and -5 mm. Interpolating, gelatin (73 mm) gets a nearly parallel face (about +2 deg) with the tip about +4 mm. Pudding (90) and sugar (92) get about +17 to +19 deg with the tip about +17 to +19 mm, which is under their 38 and 45 mm tops. Tuna (85) gets +14 deg and +14 mm against a 34 mm top. Every one of these tilts is under atan(0.5)=27 deg, and tuna's 14 deg is under atan(0.35)=19 deg. The cheaper moves are used up. Reach, groove, lip and width do not change the face angle. The long_slide was trialled 12 times and kept losing apple, potted meat and tomato soup because its rack sits in the gap. The parallelogram makes the tip rise worse (+46 mm at 85). This is the one move left in the current parts that tackles the tilt and the rise together, and it costs 18 machine minutes and $0.
risks: dice, large_marker, wood_block_cube: at 17 to 26 mm the face is now about -35 deg (bottom swung in) and the tip about 11 mm below the fixed one. On a box face the pad's tip edge touches the vertical side, so the normal stays horizontal, but the lower tip may make the fixed pad grip near the top of a 17 mm die, or put the moving tip near the table.
flat_screwdriver, golf_ball: face about -15 to -20 deg and tip about -8 mm. A round object touched below its equator gets pushed up.
mustard_bottle will probably stay failing: 96 mm is wider than the 95 mm maximum opening.
apple, tomato_soup_can, tennis_ball: their faces move closer to parallel (+2 to +20 deg) and their tips sit lower, so they should be safer.

iterations.notes:
I'm leaving the long_slide alone. It has had 12 trials and the rack in the jaw gap keeps losing apple, potted meat and tomato soup, and the fix (the outboard rack) is already recorded as an untested idea. The parallelogram makes the tip rise worse (+46 mm at 85 mm). The prismatic and the parallelogram at link_mm=50 can't open past about 59 mm.

What's left is a part of the current pads I don't see trialled in the record shown here: tilting the moving pad back (pad_angle_deg). proposals.mechanism: Two related failures. On gelatin the moving jaw squeezes the box down and out. On pudding, sugar, mustard and tuna it lands on the top face. Both come from the hinged moving jaw's fingertip rising and its face tilting as it opens. At 73 mm the moving fingertip is +15 mm above the fixed one, the gelatin's top is at +15, and the face is 47-49 deg off parallel. At 81-86 mm the tip is +20 to +26 mm, while pudding's top is at +19, tuna's at +17 and sugar's at +23; the face is 56 deg off and the contact pushes 78-84 deg down. Sliding finger mechanisms in the catalogue remove this (tip +1 mm, face 0 deg, 32 N at every opening). They were lost by a different mechanism: the rack and carriage span the jaw gap at a fixed height above the pad bottom. At reach 5 the rack hit the banana's top at +20. At reach 10-17 it hit the tomato soup can at +33, and the pads landed on top of the potted meat can (pad at +41, top at +42). At reach 22-28 the pads landed on top of the foam brick (+24, top +26) and the cup.
proposals.principle: Holding a side needs the fingertip below the object's top. A hinged finger rises by about R(1 - cos q) and turns by q, so with an 81 mm hinge radius no pad angle can be parallel and low over 17-96 mm widths: the tilt spans about 60 deg. A straight slide keeps both errors near zero at every opening. A slide only works if nothing spans the gap lower than the tallest held object (potted meat can, 84 mm) plus clearance. So the finger's clear height below the drive has to be built into the carriage, not added through long pads.
proposals.hypothesis: Every cheaper move is used up. (1) Pad parameters: 8 trials gained nothing. Pad angles of 28, 36 and 45 deg each lost banana and potted meat and gained nothing, because tilting the pad shifts the parallel opening but leaves about ±30 deg of tilt error at the ends of the width range. (2) Parallelogram: link 90 keeps the face at 0 deg, but its tip rises +46 mm at 85 mm, worse than now. Link 50 opens only 57 mm. (3) Prismatic: it opens at most 59 mm, short of the 73 mm gelatin box. (4) Long slide: about 10 trials over sector 45.4-49.5 and reach 5-27.8 would each gain 2-4 failing groups but lost 4-6 held ones. Every reach value trades the rack hitting tall objects against the pads landing on tops, and sector 50 is refused for wrist interference. (5) 12 V servos cost $68 against $40 left, and torque is not the failing mechanism: sugar needs 0.41 + 0.15*5.14 = 1.18 N*m of the 1.62 N*m stall. The missing part is a long-slide carriage with a rigid printed drop finger. The rack, sector and two 3x150 rods stay up at wrist level. The finger is part of the carriage and hangs straight down so that 95 mm below the rod and rack plane is open, and the fixed jaw gets a matching printed extension. Pads stay at reach 5 / TPU 1.5 / angle 0, the values that kept the dice, marker and wood cube. This differs from the recorded outboard-rack idea: it raises the obstruction above the gap instead of moving it sideways, and it uses only the long_slide's own rods, bushings and sector. idea.name: drop-finger long slide (rigid carriage finger hanging 95 mm below the rack/rod plane, matching fixed-jaw extension)
idea.description: This is the long_slide drive unchanged: a printed module-1 gear sector (pitch radius about 48 mm) on the gripper servo horn drives a rack on a carriage riding two 3 x 150 mm ground rods on two LM3UU bushings. All of it sits at wrist level. The moving finger is a ribbed printed PLA L-bracket screwed to the carriage. It hangs straight down so its contact face starts 95 mm below the lowest point of the rack, rods and sector, which leaves nothing spanning the jaw gap below 95 mm. It never rotates, so the face stays vertical and the tip stays level at every opening. A matching printed extension on the stock fixed jaw brings both faces to the same height. The stock pads (reach 5, TPU 1.5) screw onto both faces with the existing M2 screws. Because the finger length is built in, the pad reach stays short. That avoids the reach 22-28 failures where long pads landed on object tops. Added mass at the wrist is about 45 g, which takes about 0.07 N*m off the shoulder margin.

proposals.principle: A finger can hold a side only if, at that object's opening, its tip reaches below the top with clearance above the table. On any circular path the tip rises by about R(1-cos q), and a face that turns with its joint is parallel at only one opening. So the fix needs two things. The face orientation must stay constant (a parallelogram carrier). Diagnosis from the brief's numbers: at 85 mm the revolute gives face +44 deg and tip +26 mm. At 95 mm it gives +55 deg and +39 mm. Tuna's top is at +17 and pudding's at +19, so the tip is above the top. No catalogue part or parameter fixes this without losing held groups.
- Pads: 9 parameter-only trials gained 1 group. The tip falls only about 0.39 mm per degree of pad angle, and tuna would need about 55 deg (outside the 0-45 range). Angles of 28-45 already lost banana and potted_meat_can. A shorter reach saves only about 1.4 mm.

- Prismatic: 58 mm at most.

The new part has two elements:
1. The catalogue parallelogram at link 90 with pad_angle 0. The finger never turns, so the face stays at 0 deg at every opening. Squeeze is 19 N at 35 mm and 38 N at 85 mm, against the current 20 N.
2. On that finger, a TPU-faced pad on a vertical carriage riding two 3 mm rods in LM3UU bushings, with about 55 mm of travel and a hard lower stop. It hangs at the stop under its own weight (~10 g). On descent the table pushes it up, so its tip is always at the table no matter how far the link has swung, which cancels the +49 mm rise.
Under squeeze the horizontal load goes into the bushings and the object's weight drives the carriage against its lower stop. That gives a vertical face low on the side, opposed to the fixed jaw: antipodal. Holding check: sugar needs 5.0 N, against 2 x 0.5 x about 35 N = 35 N. Tuna needs 1.7 N, against 2 x 0.35 x 38 N = 27 N.

proposals.principle: A finger holds a side only where its contact lies below the object's top and its normal is close to horizontal. proposals.hypothesis: Every pad dimension except lip has been explored: angle (0, 14, 18, 21, 28, 36, 45), reach (0, 5) and groove (only on the slide). A 4 mm lip at the tip covers most of that gap and should take the top-edge load off the face, turning the 11-13 N downward press into a mostly lateral contact. Pudding (tip about +2 below its top) is less likely to gain. I keep angle 14 and reach 5 exactly as held, so only the lip changes.
